articles.title: Your Eval Suite Has a Flake Rate: Gating LLM Changes on Paired, Powered Tests
articles.excerpt: I have watched the same release go wrong three times. Someone tunes a prompt or swaps a model, the eval average moves from 0.81 to 0.83, the PR gets approved, and two weeks later a specific intent is…
articles.body: I have watched the same release go wrong three times. Someone tunes a prompt or swaps a model, the eval average moves from 0.81 to 0.83, the PR gets approved, and two weeks later a specific intent is failing in production. The regression was real. The improvement was not. Nobody did anything careless — the eval reported a number that looked like a measurement and was actually a coin flip. The unglamorous part of LLMOps is not prompt management or tracing. It is that most eval suites cannot detect the changes teams ship on. Fixing that is a half-day of statistics and one CI job. Three kinds of noise, only one of which is your change Before you compare two configurations, know what is moving: Example sampling noise. Your golden set has 200 examples. Each one is worth 0.5 points.

articles.body: msiexec repair mode resolves a binary path from a directory an installer wrote to Windows Installer supports a repair operation that restores missing or modified files for an installed product. Repair is driven by the installation database, and the repair process has to find the source files it needs. That resolution step is where this class of issue lives. The mechanism, stated carefully During a repair, msiexec reads the product database and attempts to source the components it must restore. When the original source media is unavailable, Windows Installer can fall back to locations it considers valid, including cached package data and directories resolved from the installation context.

articles.title: Failure Detection and Recovery in Healthcare Agentic Workflows
articles.excerpt: Agentic healthcare systems often coordinate several dependent operations. A failure in one step can prevent the entire workflow from reaching its intended outcome. Examples include rejected referrals,…
articles.body: Agentic healthcare systems often coordinate several dependent operations. A failure in one step can prevent the entire workflow from reaching its intended outcome. Examples include rejected referrals, unavailable services, missing authorization, incomplete records, and repeated communication failures. A robust agent architecture should distinguish between transient errors, recoverable failures, and conditions that require human intervention. Transient errors may justify bounded retries with appropriate backoff. Recoverable failures may require additional information or an alternative authorized pathway. Persistent or clinically consequential failures should trigger escalation. Workflow state should remain observable throughout this process.

articles.title: Assembly required
articles.excerpt: A cloud hands you IP ranges, security groups, service accounts, IAM policies, Count the objects in the smallest useful deployment. One container serving HTTP, On AWS: a VPC, two subnets in two availab…
articles.body: A cloud hands you IP ranges, security groups, service accounts, IAM policies, load balancer listeners and virtual machines. None of those is a place to put an application. You get to one by assembling them, and the assembly is work: a few days at the start of a project, an hour or two a week after that, for as long as the project lives. It bills nothing. It ships no feature. Each team that does it builds a private platform-as-a-service out of the same parts, and the one they finish is as good as their best engineer's spare attention, which is not very good. The other option is to pay an infrastructure salary for the same artifact. The not-so-fun puzzle Count the objects in the smallest useful deployment. One container serving HTTP, one Postgres behind it, on a domain, with TLS.

articles.title: Two strangers' repos, deployed by agents, unaided
articles.excerpt: The claim this platform is built on is that a coding agent can take an application So: two repositories found on GitHub, cloned cold, neither of them ours and gg skill and Both of them got there. the…
articles.body: The claim this platform is built on is that a coding agent can take an application to production on its own. That is easy to demonstrate on our own code, which is exactly why demonstrating it on our own code proves nothing. So: two repositories found on GitHub, cloned cold, neither of them ours and neither of them seen before. One a Node service with a Python ML sidecar, the other a .NET 8 app that needs Postgres. Two agents, each given the gg skill and nothing else — no runbook, no hints, and nobody to ask. Both of them got there. the repo outcome wall clock gg calls Node + Python ML sidecar 1/1, verified serving 15m20s 19, zero errors .NET 8 + Postgres 1/1, verified serving 24m36s ~48, half of them polls The part worth more than the times: neither agent accepted 1/1 as proof.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
